title: The Growing Threat to Executive and Expert Careers
author: Colin Gautrey
source: Gautrey Life (gautrey.life), via the Radical Conformity Substack, November 1, 2026
summary: Colin Gautrey, an executive coach who writes on power and influence, argues that senior executives and established experts face mounting pressure from AI, geopolitical and institutional disruption, and a widening gap between what they must understand and what their existing knowledge and intelligence sources let them see. He says working harder, gaining another qualification or learning a few AI tools is not an adequate response. He proposes a four-part journey: the independence to see clearly (Radical Conformity), the breadth to understand the wider terrain (Domain Mastery), the capacity to decide without certainty (Astute Judgement), and the ability to move complex human systems toward results (Political Dexterity). He introduces the Galileo Dilemma, in which the change a system needs threatens the very system through which it must be achieved. He ends with a vision of AI-enabled executives who use AI intelligently while keeping responsibility for their own decisions. The closing third describes his Pattern Recognition System, private coaching and ExecutiveDM service, so the piece is partly a framework statement and partly a promotion of his own offerings.
points: Expertise is becoming easier to reproduce and challenge, since anyone with an AI assistant can produce a plausible alternative to a senior judgement.
The real danger for senior leaders is no longer not knowing enough but not knowing what they need to know, which calls for wider field of vision and better questions.
Waiting for certainty can be as dangerous as acting too soon, so leaders must separate reliable evidence from plausible speculation and stay ready to adjust.
The Galileo Dilemma names the situation where the change an organization needs threatens the system through which it must be delivered, and more evidence or authority alone will not resolve it.
The author's ideal is the AI-enabled executive who uses the tools intelligently but never surrenders responsibility for judgement.
quotes: Senior experts face a different version of the same problem. The knowledge and experience that established their value are becoming easier to access, reproduce and challenge.
Even sound judgements are more vulnerable to scrutiny. Anyone with an AI assistant can produce a plausible alternative, whether or not they understand the underlying problem.

The answer is not simply to work harder, acquire another qualification or learn a few new AI tools. It requires a different approach to understanding the world, making decisions and exercising influence.
The danger is no longer simply not knowing enough. It is not knowing what you need to know.

Waiting for certainty can become as dangerous as acting prematurely. The challenge is to distinguish reliable evidence from plausible speculation, recognise competing explanations and understand the implications of different choices.

AI can contribute enormously to this process. It can challenge assumptions, examine alternatives and expose weaknesses in an argument. But it can also generate convincing errors and misleading confidence.

More argument, more evidence or greater formal authority may not resolve the problem. You need to understand how the system actually operates, anticipate its responses and create conditions in which progress becomes possible.
Not executives who surrender their judgement to AI, but those who use it intelligently while retaining responsibility for their decisions.
